summary: Specifies 6to4, an interim way for IPv6 sites to talk to each other across the IPv4 Internet without setting up tunnels by hand, and to reach native IPv6 networks through relay routers. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Two houses with new phone lines can talk through the old phone network if the new calls are tucked inside old ones. 6to4 does this for the new Internet addresses.

questions: how to connect ipv6 over ipv4 automatically
subtitle: How an IPv6 site can reach other IPv6 sites across plain IPv4, with no tunnel to set up, by hiding the IPv4 address inside the IPv6 prefix.

tldr.problem: Isolated IPv6 sites on a network with no native IPv6 support need to talk to each other, and to native IPv6 networks, without hand-configured tunnels.
tldr.mechanism: Any site with a globally unique IPv4 address gets the IPv6 prefix 2002:V4ADDR::/48, and its border router wraps IPv6 packets in IPv4 packets (protocol 41) addressed to the IPv4 address found inside the destination prefix. Relay routers connect 6to4 sites to native IPv6.
tldr.outcome: It gives a site an interim, globally unique IPv6 prefix with minimal configuration. The RFC calls it an interim start-up tool and expects sites to move to native IPv6 when their ISP offers it.

today: RFC 3056 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself presents 6to4 as an optional interim transition mechanism, not a permanent solution.

sections.title: An Interim Bridge Between IPv6 and IPv4
sections.content:
RFC 3056 specifies 6to4, an optional interim mechanism that lets IPv6 sites talk to each other over the IPv4 network without explicit tunnel setup. It also lets them reach native IPv6 domains through relay routers. Effectively, the wide area IPv4 network is treated as a unicast point-to-point link layer.

The RFC is clear that this is a start-up transition tool for the period when IPv4 and IPv6 co-exist, and that it is not a permanent solution. Sites should migrate to native IPv6 prefixes when possible, which is as soon as the site's ISP offers native IPv6 connectivity.

The mechanism works for sites rather than individual hosts, and is implemented almost entirely in border routers. Hosts need no specific modification except a suggested address selection default. It does not need IPv4-compatible IPv6 addresses or configured tunnels.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine two new playgrounds with only an old road between them. 6to4 is a trick for sending kids between the playgrounds on the old road until a proper new road is built.

sections.title: The 6to4 Address Prefix
sections.content:
A site with at least one valid, globally unique 32-bit IPv4 address (called V4ADDR) is automatically deemed to have an IPv6 prefix. The address MUST be properly allocated to the site and MUST NOT be a private address. IANA permanently assigned the 13-bit Top Level Aggregator value 0x0002 to 6to4, which is 2002::/16 as an IPv6 prefix.

The site's prefix is 48 bits long: 2002:V4ADDR::/48. After it come a 16-bit Site Level Aggregator ID and a 64-bit Interface ID. This has exactly the same format as normal /48 prefixes, so inside the site it works like any other IPv6 prefix. If the IPv4 address is dynamic, the IPv6 prefix is dynamic too, with the same lifetime.

For example, the IPv4 address 192.1.2.3 gives the prefix 2002:c001:0203::/48, and 9.254.253.252 gives 2002:09fe:fdfc::/48.

When a host has both a 6to4 and a native address, address selection matters. If one host has only a 6to4 address, the 6to4 address should be used for both ends. If both have both kinds, either 6to4 or native should be used for both, the choice should be configurable, and the default should be native IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: Your house number on the old street is copied into your new address. So anyone who sees the new address can read off the old house number and know where to send things.

sections.title: Encapsulation in IPv4
sections.content:
When IPv6 packets leave a 6to4 site over its external IPv4 connection, they are placed inside IPv4 packets with IPv4 protocol type 41, the same value assigned for IPv6 tunneled inside IPv4. The IPv4 body holds the IPv6 header and payload. The encapsulation point acts like an IPv6 interface whose link layer is the IPv4 network; the RFC calls it a pseudo-interface, and V4ADDR MUST be configured on the IPv4 interface.

The IPv4 Time to Live and the IPv6 hop limit are set as normal. Neighbor Unreachability Detection and link-local addresses follow the transition mechanisms RFC, RFC 2893, although the RFC knows of no scenario where a link-local address on this pseudo-interface would be useful.

On packet size, MTU handling is as for tunnels in RFC 2893. If the IPv6 MTU is too large for some IPv4 subnet, IPv4 fragmentation follows. The IPv4 "do not fragment" bit SHOULD NOT be set on the encapsulating packet.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like putting a letter in a bigger envelope so the old post office can carry it. At the other end, someone opens the big envelope and takes out the letter.

sections.title: Sending and Decapsulation Rules
sections.content:
The only change to standard IPv6 forwarding is a pair of rules that every 6to4 router, and only 6to4 routers, MUST implement. They apply only at border routers, and no IPv4 routing information is imported into IPv6 routing, or the other way round.

The sending rule: if the next hop IPv6 address matches 2002::/16 and does not match any prefix of the local site, apply any security checks, encapsulate the packet in IPv4 with the destination set to the V4ADDR taken from the next hop address, and queue it for IPv4 forwarding. If the final destination is not a 6to4 address and not local, the next hop will be the 6to4 address of a relay router.

The decapsulation rule for incoming IPv4 packets with protocol type 41: apply any security checks, remove the IPv4 header, and submit the packet to local IPv6 routing.

In the simple scenario, any number of 6to4 sites can interoperate with no tunnel configuration. All that is needed is the right DNS entries and these two rules in the 6to4 router. Each site should use only one IPv4 address per 6to4 router, namely the one on the router's external interface.
sections.plainLanguage: The router at the edge does two jobs. Going out, it puts the letter in the big envelope and reads the old house number from the address. Coming in, it opens the big envelope and hands over the letter.

sections.title: Relay Routers and Routing
sections.content:
To reach native IPv6 networks, 6to4 sites use a relay router: a 6to4 router that also has a native IPv6 interface. There are two ways to run the 6to4 exterior routing domain. Either no exterior routing protocol is used and each 6to4 router has a default IPv6 route to the relay router, or an IPv6 exterior protocol such as BGP4+ is used, which gives policy control over which 6to4 routers may use which relay.

A relay router MUST advertise a route to 2002::/16 into the native IPv6 routing domain, with its reach limited by routing policy. Prefixes more specific than that must not be propagated. A 6to4 site with a native connection MUST NOT advertise its 2002::/48 prefix there, and native IPv6 operators MUST filter out any 2002:: advertisement longer than /16.

A site that has both kinds of interface but is unwilling to relay MUST NOT advertise any 2002:: prefix natively, and MUST NOT advertise native prefixes or a default route into the 6to4 domain.

One dangerous misconfiguration is advertising 2002::/16 into a 6to4 exterior routing domain, which would attract all 6to4 traffic and cause a loop; this MUST NOT be done. The RFC also warns that if the IPv4 world is fragmented into disjoint networks, the 6to4 world is fragmented too, and sites on one side cannot reach sites on the other through different relays.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay router is a friendly translator standing at the border between the old and new neighborhoods. It must tell only the new neighborhood where the old one is, and never confuse the old one by pointing it back at itself.

sections.title: NAT, Multihoming and Moving to Native IPv6
sections.content:
6to4 works with a firewall at the border router. With an IPv4 NAT, the NAT box must also be a full IPv6 router with 6to4, using its globally unique IPv4 address as V4ADDR. Every host behind it can then become an IPv6 host with a globally unique /48 prefix, and no address translation is needed for the IPv6 traffic. If a host is several NATs away, only the outermost NAT, which owns the unique IPv4 address, does the encapsulation. 6to4 can also co-exist with Realm-Specific IP (RSIP), and can be used inside a private corporate network, where V4ADDR MUST be a duly allocated global IPv4 address that is unique within that network.

Sites multihomed on IPv4 MAY use a 2002:: prefix for each IPv4 border router, giving a simple form of IPv6 multihoming.

The RFC lays out a five-step path from 6to4 to native IPv6: run IPv6 on the site, configure a 6to4 border router and DNS entries, find a relay, add a second native prefix when native connectivity arrives, and finally remove the 6to4 configuration once its use has ceased, which may be several years later.
sections.plainLanguage: You can start using the bridge today, even from behind a shared front door, and later when the new road is finished you keep both for a while and then stop using the bridge.

sections.title: Security and Other Considerations
sections.content:
Implementors must consider attacks against IPv4 as well as IPv6. The RFC advises against using IP security at both levels for efficiency, but notes that IPv4 security will not protect IPv6 traffic once it leaves the 6to4 domain, so IPv6 security is required even if IPv4 security exists.

By default, 6to4 traffic is accepted and decapsulated from any source from which regular IPv4 traffic is accepted. Extra source filtering may be applied, such as checking that the encapsulating IPv4 address is consistent with the encapsulated 2002:: address, with exceptions for relay routers. Any 6to4 traffic whose source or destination embeds a V4ADDR that is not a global unicast address MUST be silently discarded by encapsulators and decapsulators. This rules out private, broadcast, subnet broadcast, multicast and loopback addresses.

Other points: 6to4 assumes only unicast in the IPv4 network, so an IPv6 multicast routing protocol is needed. ICMP errors from IPv4 often cannot be turned into ICMPv6 messages, so the IPv4 network looks like an undiagnosable link layer. The IANA needs no assignments beyond the already assigned TLA value 0x0002.
sections.plainLanguage: The router should refuse mail that claims to come from a made-up or obviously wrong old address. And the letter inside still needs its own lock, because the big envelope is only protection on part of the trip.

fields.desc: The site's globally unique IPv4 address.

fields.desc: Site Level Aggregator ID, for subnets within the site.

fields.name: Interface ID
fields.desc: Identifies the interface within the subnet.
